#4075. Mailbox: Ocarina Intruders, Pikmin Day, Too Many Humans - Nintendo Life Letters

Hello, you. Yes, you. It's just us here today - everyone else is busy in Hyrule or Leonida right now.

In fact, it's been like that for most of the month, it seems, as the Nintendo Life Mailbox is looking pretty empty! So, it'll be a nice quick one this month. We'll have you back with your preferred ride — equine or automotive — in a jiffy.

Got something you want to get off your chest? Remember, we're ready and waiting to read about your game-related ponderings as we head into the holidays. Each month we’ll highlight a Star Letter, the writer of which will receive a month’s subscription to our ad-free Supporter scheme. Check out the submission guidelines at the bottom of this page.

So, let's slice open our correspondence...

I've been inspired to share in this letter about my first encounter with The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time following the feature you ran on this very topic, because it's a touching, unique story.

I was about 11 years old in 1998 and had been avidly following OoT in the magazines, absorbing every screenshot and article about this sword and shield weilding greened tuniced hero.

Bizarrely I'd never played a Zelda game before but something about it looked magical and exciting. So I did what any 11 year old would do. I asked for the game for Christmas.

So, Christmas morning arrives and I excitedly tumble down the stairs to the presents under the tree. I open them all but.... There's a pang of absence. No Zelda game. Where is it I exclaim!? And my mum sheepishly informs me that it didn't arrive in time for Christmas.

I cry. Real tears. I'm distraught. Inconsolable. For months I've waited for this amazing looking game and I can't play it.

What happened next is... I think... wonderful parenting.

While I was busy in my bedroom creating my own water temple with more tears than a kingdom (see what I did there?), my mum phones every parent of my school friends she knows until she finds someone with a copy of Zelda. And eventually, she does. She creeps up to knock on my door and says "Hey, Listen! I'll take you to your friends place, he has a copy"

And so, my tears stop and off I go to watch my pal play the game and suddenly a terrible Christmas becomes a brilliant one. The game is everything I imagine it to be and more and my mate and I spend hours solving Deku Tree puzzles and gasping at Hyrule Field's majesty.

So as we all enjoy the remake of Ocarina of Time decades later, I just have one thing to say: Thanks mum. You understood the stakes and you cared enough to help me get my Zelda fix that fateful Christmas of 1998.

And ever since that day, my life has been met with the least terrible of fates: I became a huge fan of Zelda and have bought every single one since on day one - no more painful Christmas mornings! YoshiTails

That is some above-and-beyond parenting, Mrs YoshiTails! We salute you.

I'm imagining what my mum would have said to some random mother ringing her on Christmas morning, asking if their kid could come over to play a video game. I assume she would have reacted in the classic British manner: agreeing to it with bemusement while silently seething, resenting the interloper for every surrendered mince pie.

I joke! I had no friends. I did have Zelda, though. - Ed.

Community "I Think Of Her Every Time I Play It" - Your Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Memories

We seem to have sleepwalked into an era of walking simulators.

I’m not talking about artsy indie games emphasising investigation over action, but big budget AAA titles starring main “characters” who look like they’ve walked out of a Hollywood movie. There are too many humans in games and it’s stifling the medium.

Back when the mascot character was king, protagonists felt properly differentiated both aesthetically and mechanically: Mario jumps, Sonic runs, Spyro flies, Crash bangs and wallops. Of these, only Mario could be called ‘human’, and even he has about as much in common with a real plumber as Sonic does with a real hedgehog.

Vibrant colours and exaggerated movements helped make the games legible on small screens when pixels, polygons and processing power came at a premium, and this gave games a unique vibe and feel. Now that we can better render humans in all their hairy, fleshy complexity, video game aesthetics have moved from ‘cartoonish’ to ‘cinematic’, and physics have followed suit.

Thing is, if I wanted to control a human, I’d put the controller down and go for a walk. (…Maybe not a bad idea actually). We’re meandering, clunky lumps of meat who navigate the world in a most pedestrian manner. Fine for a trip to the shops. Not the most inspiring thing to control in a video game.

It should be said that the ‘mascot character’ isn’t completely dead. The House of Mario was built by pixelated protags who carry the forward the flame of the 8-bit era. The portly purported plumber is still as satisfyingly springy as ever. DK has swapped pixels for vowels but continues to dish out delightful destruction like a primate possessed. Even the new squid-kids on the block - Splatoon’s Inklings - are unashamedly ‘gamey’, slipping slickly through their own mercurial fluids.

It’s a pleasant reminder that video games let us be anything we want: a bird (Untitled Goose Game), a plane (Star Fox) or even a kickflipping train (Denshattack). With that in mind, it seems a shame to be stuck as the same humdrum human that AAA titles insist on lumbering us with.

As film studios conglomerate and cinematic universes bleed into each other, I wish video games would embrace what makes them unique rather than dissolving into the same great multimedia melange. I’ve had enough of the homogeneous Homo sapiens-centric pseudo-cinema now synonymous with AAA game development and wish that more creative energies would be put into games that actually push the mechanical possibilities of the medium.

I disagree, purely because there are just so many games of all flavours out there. If you want to be a squirrel or a crab or an insect or anything else, there's never been a better time. Big, small, there's just so much incredible variety. If AAA isn't doing it for you, the other As have got you covered.

I get the sense perhaps you're reacting to the priority of animation over gamefeel in some cases - lumpy realistic animation versus snappy response? Pushing right on the stick and a moment later a soupy animation cycle transitions into the movement you've input (as opposed to Mario or Link responding instantly, if unrealistically).

If that's the case, I agree that Nintendo's approach is my preference, whatever form of animal, vegetable or mineral you're controlling. The animation of an Assassin's Creed or a GTA is incredibly impressive, but it's interminably slow if you're coming to it with a Mario mindset. I find I have to be invested in the cinema and 'show' of those games if they're going to click. My all-time favourites tend to have much more responsive controls, though. - Ed.

When Nintendo announced Pikmin Day this year for November 1st, it seemed to me that it was met with mixed reactions. People said that saying 11/1 looks like Pikmin is a bit of a stretch, and they didn't really announce anything particularly interesting. While this is true, I found it positively delightful, specifically the second half of the direct when Fuka Koshiba was revealed to be hired by Nintendo. While their conversation was a bit awkward (as Nintendo Direct dialogue always is), I thought it was super cool that they hired her just from seeing her posts on Instagram. And I've been loving the charming shorts that they've been releasing recently. And I'm not even a big Pikmin fan!

The direct was weird, certainly unnecessary, and a bit awkward, but that's what made it amazing. It was delightfully quirky, dumb, delightful, and wholly Nintendo.

I think any rational person will have responded to the 'Pikmin Day' declaration in the same way: wut. Anyone but Nintendo would have been torn to absolute shreds.

Frankly, though, with everything else going on in the world, if Shigsy wants to claim some random day for what might be their best series, crack on. A '1' looks like a Pikmin, you say, Miyamoto-san? Sure, fine. So, Pikmin 5 announcement next November, hmm? - Ed.

"For Pokémon day next year, I want a Pok" - Scottdevine53

#4074. Quantic Dream addresses toxicity, tech bugs and tutorials for Spellcasters Chronicles closed beta 2 - here's how to get a key

Here are the start and end times for the second Spellcasters Chronicles closed beta, as well as what's new in this latest test.

Quantic Dream has opened up its upcoming fantasy MOBA for a second closed beta weekend starting from today, January 29, until 9AM UTC on Monday February 2.

The closed beta is for PC only in Europe, Asia and North America and potential players can register to join the waitlist for a key at the game’s official website or on the Spellcasters Chronicles Steam page. Players who had access to the first closed beta will automatically have access to the second, but you can sign up on both the site and Steam to increase your chances of entry.

The MOBA genre is competitive in every sense and Quantic Dream is trying to break into it with a Magic the Gathering-esque spin on the format. Players build a deck of cards before queuing into teams of 3, then face off as battling mages, summoning creatures, building fortifications and casting spells rather than choosing a Hero with unique abilities in the traditional MOBA style.

Beta content includes a new map, 6 new spells and 5 new summon creatures for your deck, as well as 3 new buildings too.

Also new for this second closed beta is an introduction and tutorial for some of the game’s finer details, as well as a text chat for strategising and much-needed player reporting system to go with it. It will also feature early versions of the Spellcaster customisation system and ranked matches.

Quantic Dream has said that this closed beta places a strong emphasis on performance, memory usage and overall gameplay stability to create a smoother experience, so with that in mind, here are the minimum and recommended PC specs:

Spellcasters Chronicles is the first ever multiplayer online game from Quantic Dream, the French studio best known for cinematic narrative games like Detroit: Become Human, Heavy Rain and Beyond: Two Souls.

A TV adaptation of the latter game is reportedly in development, or the rights for one have been acquired at least. Elsewhere, Quantic Dream’s long-rumoured game in the Star Wars franchise was revealed as Star Wars Eclipse, a return-to-type narrative action game set in the High Republic era of a galaxy far, far away.

#4071. Talking Point: How Often Are You Willing To Play Games At 30FPS?

While GTA 6 has been receiving unbelievable praise and is technically considered one of the best video games of all time according to Metacritic, that certainly doesn't mean it's immune to criticism.

One of the big talking points both before and after launch has been that it's a 30FPS experience across all Xbox and PlayStation consoles, and if you're going from 60FPS back to 30FPS, there's definitely an adjustment period. Some people are absolutely fine with that, while others are finding it extremely difficult to go back.

For what it's worth, our friends at Digital Foundry have been analysing this in depth today:

Feature Why Isn't Grand Theft Auto 6 60fps?

Digital FoundryAnd could frame generation be the solution?

Rockstar Games has already confirmed recently that even the PS5 Pro doesn't come close to running GTA 6 at 60FPS due to the system's processor not being powerful enough, so we might be forced to wait until the next generation of consoles (and PC) before the game will become playable at 60 frames per-second.

"The PS5 Pro features an upgraded graphics processor and upscaling technology that we leverage to increase the game’s visual fidelity. While the PS5 Pro’s central processor is slightly better than the PS5 base console, it is not powerful enough to run the game’s complex simulation at higher frame rates.”

With all of this in mind, we're interested to hear what you think about playing games at 30FPS on Xbox, PlayStation or anywhere else. It's becoming much more common that 60FPS is the default these days, but there are still some phenomenal 30FPS-only experiences out there, and it's a shame to think people are missing out on them.

I personally much prefer playing at 60FPS if I can, and there are certain games I will avoid at 30FPS until they get a patch down the line (like Mafia: Definitive Edition), but when it comes to industry-defining masterpieces like Red Dead Redemption 2 and Grand Theft Auto VI, the last thing I'd want is for them to scale back the detail in order to squeeze in a 60FPS mode.

News GTA 6 Comparison Shows Difference Between Xbox Series X And Series S

Here's how Grand Theft Auto 6 looks across both Xbox consoles

News Three Big Takeaways From Digital Foundry's GTA 6 Analysis For Xbox Series X|S

So, what do you think? Tell us in the poll above and in the comments section below.

Fraser is the News Editor at Pure Xbox, where he spends his time reporting on the biggest stories in the world of Xbox and beyond.

@PSbox I played these on a 1080p Flatscreen TV - the same Brand TV I have today and basically the same technology that all LED TV's these days have - although now I have an OLED with much higher refresh rate and VRR capability - but back then, the Flatscreen TV's were 'new' technology and replaced the CRT.

Its basically the exact same technology that modern Flat screen TV's use. They've arguably got better today at 30fps because they have higher refresh rates and of course far better Gaming modes too with superior response times.

You could argue that Goldeneye and Perfect Dark on the N64 were using 'CRT' TV's rather than Flat Screen technology that replaced them. Those games were the HD Flatscreen PS3/360 era games, the era that the large screen TV's came in and the first few generations of the technology that modern 4k TV's use today, the exact same method of displaying frames as today with less capable image processing and motion handling due to weaker chips and software.

As I said, they probably were worse at handling 30fps than modern 4k VRR enabled TV's we have today because they were the newest technology.

I also preferred to play Forza Horizon at 30fps because the visual trade off for 60fps was far too big a sacrifice and the game didn't feel or respond any worse. Forza Horizon was always a locked 30fps and felt extremely smooth and responsive to me. 60fps didn't make any 'noticeable' difference to the gameplay and feel, the handling etc but looked significantly worse so the decision to play at 30fps was an easy one!

I just Googled "why do modern tvs play 30 fps worse" and the search results corroborate this. Modern screens are essentially too fast to display 30 fps effectively. I have an OLED which explains why I find 30 fps to be rubbish for certain games. @PSbox Both things at the same time! There are people in denial because their favourite games are 30fps (or lower) like the examples I posted, people who really are fine with slow frame transition and even poor pacing, and people like us whose brain is more sensitive to the frame rate, frame pacing and camera, and can feel sick. I have noticed that the camera has a lot to do with it, e.g., Crash Bandicoot N.sane Trilogy vs. Spyro Reignited Trilogy, the former being much more tolerable. These factors are more noticeable in new, faster TVs. I also notice the difference between 60 and 120 as smoother, but I don't select 120 because it's unnecessary to lower the resolution or image quality for that extra polish in the transition of frames. Being 30fps-tolerant would be an advantage for gaming, but we are not rare, I just asked Bing:

120–144 Hz → major improvement in smoothness and responsiveness

360–500 Hz → diminishing returns, but some users still perceive differences in latency and motion clarity

High-refresh displays (90–144Hz) make low framerates feel worse because the contrast is more obvious.

OLED screens reduce motion blur, making stutter more noticeable.

Poor frame pacing (uneven frame delivery) can feel worse than a stable 30fps.

Short answer: A large portion of the gaming community can detect and be bothered by framerates under 60fps.

@PSbox Modern TV's refer to the Fat screen Technology by which your OLED and 4K LCD TV's all use. The 'older' technology they are referring to is the CRT Era, the N64 Goldeneye/Perfect Dark era.

The PS3/360 era is the era of the 'modern' TV technology.

I have a far bigger issue with uneven frame rate or uneven frame delivery than a stable, locked 30fps. 30fps isn't an issue unless you have uneven frame pacing. I'd rather have a consistent Frame rate than tearing and stutter/judder caused by frame rate drops - which VRR can help with nowadays but wasn't available on a TV until relatively recently.

But VRR, 4k 120hz etc are just the advancement of 'modern' TV's that replaced the CRT technology that ALL Domestic TV's were before they were replaced by Modern TV's. The very first Gaming Consoles and Home Computers were plugged into CRT TV's and 'Modern' TV's refer to the HD Flat Screen TV era and onwards that replaced the CRT TV's.

Your OLED uses the exact same 'Modern' technology and method of display as the HD TV's of the 360/PS3 era, the era of games like BioShock, Uncharted, Last of Us, Gears of War, Mass Effect etc etc - ALL Game of the Year winners and that also continued with the PS4/XB1 gen and games like the Witcher 3, Horizon Zero Dawn (PS4 and PS4 Pro) and God of War (PS4, PS4 Pro was 40-60fps in performance mode).

Point is, ALL games in the 'Modern TV' era that have been Game of the Year winners have predominantly been 30fps - RDR and RDR2, as well as GTA have always been (or targeted) 30fps (inc games like Assassins Creed, Dead Space etc). Its only when those 'old' games get brought forward to 'new' hardware that they target 60fps because the new Hardware isn't as CPU or GPU Limited as the Consoles they were built for. Bloodborne is another example of a 30fps game and award winning - built for hardware designed to use 'Modern' TV's like your OLED and won awards on Console connected to 'modern' TV's too

#4070. Feature: A Lost Box Restored My Faith In Zelda's Staying Power

A few weeks ago, my brother sent me a photo with zero context. He was at our parents’ house, helping them pack up for a cross-country move, when he found something unusual: a heavy metal box with a latch.

It took me a second to dust off the cobwebs in that corner of my mind, but once I did, I recognised the box as the promotional material Nintendo sent me back in 1998 to celebrate the original release of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

I asked my bro what was inside the box and a few moments later he replied with another picture. The box was empty.

I can’t think of anything more depressing than an empty treasure chest. All the anticipation leading to… crushing disappointment. Anyone who ever slogged through the Phoenix Cave in Final Fantasy VI knows the feeling.

This chest originally housed a pre-launch, gold N64 cart of Ocarina of Time. It was Nintendo’s not-so-subtle message that this game was a treasure. A bit on the nose, but the zeitgeist of an entire generation of gamers has certainly proven them right. OoT is a treasure.

In this case, I can at least take solace knowing that I'm the one who emptied the chest and thoroughly enjoyed its golden treasure. The empty box is evidence of that.

My brother’s timing was impeccable — bordering on eerie — unearthing the box less than a week before the Switch 2 remake launched.

Like many of you, my son (let's call him Tim) and I were eagerly awaiting the OoT remake. He hadn’t played the original, but is an avid Zelda fan, particularly the modern titles. I knew I’d love the Remake, but I was a bit nervous that he would have a different reaction. He’s a member of this Breath of the Wild, open-world generation, after all. Would the old-school Zelda formula appeal to his generation, or would it die with mine?

As they say, sometimes one man’s treasure is another man’s trash.

My love for Zelda, and desire to pass it down to my son, parallels the experience my father had with his four boys. Dad loved to work with his hands and my brothers and I were always enlisted in projects: everything from clearing the land, felling trees, reroofing the house, building an addition, repainting, and working on a long series of rundown cars. He made sure we received hands-on working experience.

Right around the time I received the Zelda Treasure Chest, my dad began restoring classic Ford Mustangs in his garage. I had already moved out, but my youngest brother ( the one who found the chest) was there to be Dad’s understudy. Together they restored two beautiful Mustangs, allowing my dad to share his love for mechanical craft and manual labour.

Sharing an old classic is one thing, but actually passing down a passion depends on how well the original holds up to modern sensibilities.

A restored car regains its iconic look, but it will also retain the old feel, complete with stiff brakes and crank windows. After all, restoring something doesn’t place it in a state opposite to its nature. A 1967 Mustang GT Fastback is a 1967 Mustang GT Fastback only if it looks, sounds, and feels like a 1967 Mustang GT Fastback, for better or worse.

Media remakes and remasters are often criticised for following this type of approach. Shot-for-shot remakes come across as unnecessary cash grabs (looking at you Disney) while complete reimaginings seem to either spectacularly succeed (Dune, Casino Royale, Metroid Zero Mission) or fail (Planet of the Apes 2001, Secret of Mana, Quantum Leap).

Like my old man, Nintendo’s philosophy seems closer to restoration than reimagining. Star Fox and Super Mario RPG are recent examples, with the slightly more ambitious Link’s Awakening preceding them by a few years. There are many others.

In each case, the spirit of the original is preserved while a few quality-of-life improvements are added. And of course, each old classic receives a new coat of paint.

By taking this approach, Nintendo has been careful to avoid the pitfalls that so many media companies encounter when updating beloved products. Their roster of remakes have largely avoided any 'Han shot first' controversies. Thank goodness.

A philosophy of preserving the original’s frame, while souping up the engine, allows old and new players to enjoy the gaming experience without fighting retro clunkiness.

So, what does Tim think of Ocarina of Time?

He loves it, of course! And it’s been immensely satisfying to see him enjoy it. Confirmation bias can be a wonderful thing.

The wife and I have a ritual of playing Zelda games together, so we’re playing it in short, infrequent bursts. I’m not complaining, as it’s allowed me to savour the experience. Tim, on the other hand, is powering through it at a much faster pace. He also spectates while my wife and I play. We always aim for a 100% run, so Tim takes notes on all of the heart pieces and bag upgrades he missed.

I’m just excited to see my son enjoying a game I grew up with. My dad passed on his love for mechanical craft to his boys, and I’m sharing my passion for sidequests with mine.

It’s been a good month. It began with a nostalgic relic and a bit of disappointment (grr, I still can’t find that gold cart), but also included a timeless masterpiece that’s been successfully passed to the next generation.

30 years ago my dad shared the muscle cars from his youth. This year I got to share a classic Zelda adventure from mine.

I wonder what treasure my boy will pass on to his kids in 30 years' time.

Have you successfully passed a favourite game down to the next generation? Was it the original, or a remake that added modern improvements? Share your stories in the comments below.

#4069. Infinity Nikki ushers in the Year of the Horse with... a deer-themed Version 2.2

Chromatic Beings Everbright, the latest major Infinity Nikki update, has arrived, bringing Chinese New Year celebrations vibe to the game.

Infinity Nikki, the free-to-play, open-world dress-up RPG, has delivered yet another big content drop in the form of Chromatic Beings Everbright. The latest update brings the game up to version 2.2, and introduces a new narrative chapter, and gameplay taking place around a festival narrative.

If you couldn’t guess already, the new theme is Bloom Festival, inspired by Chinese New Year celebrations.

The big new story chapter takes place in the Infinity Nikki’s Wanxiang Realm. This deceptively serene and blissful region hides a dark secret, however. Chromafaces, the mythical inhabitants of the realm, have to embody fixed identities that dictate how they live and work.

These are doled out through Character Tokens, which are used to assign roles to each individual. The story follows Nikki as she uncovers the script that runs the realm and the facade it props up. Nikki will help free Chromafaces and dispel the illusion.

The Wanxiang Realm is split into three areas. Cai Ye is your typical lantern-lit district, where festivals and fireworks happen. Kongming Gorge is almost the opposite of that; a quiet and cold place. Finally, Jiuhua Pavilion literally floats above the region, and it's home to neverending music and dance.

The other big addition in 2.2 are the two new 5-Star Resonance Outfits with some interesting gameplay implications. Where Wanxiang Weaves Life is inspired by wuxia aesthetics, and true to its inspirations, it lets Nikki shapeshift into different Spirit Personas - and automatically collect resources in her vicinity.

Chroma's Mortal Heart, on the other hand, allows Nikki to fly around the Wanxiang Realm, drawing on the power of the Celestial Deer. This outfit also uses Celestial Deer Vision to automatically ping and mark treasure chests around her.

You can also look forward to Nefarious Shadows, a new Ability Outfit, which lets Nikki see through disguises, and reveals hidden paths in the world.

As with every major update, of course, there are themed activities and limited-time events throughout. Hotpot House is a cooking minigame where you attempt to run the eponymous restaurant, whereas Flavor Frenzy is series of platforming challenges that tasks you with gathering ingredients. Fortune Mahjong is a little more straightforward, with support for solo and multiplayer play.

If you’re jumping back into the game soon, be sure to hit up our Infinity Nikki codes page for some freebies.

#4067. How To Get Your Free Snom Ornament From The Pokemon Center

Between games, plushes, and trading cards, being a Pokemon fan can get pretty pricey. That’s why it’s always welcome when The Pokemon Company gives its fans something for free, and if you’ve got more merch to buy heading into the holidays, then there might be a new ornament waiting for you when you head to the Pokemon Center checkout.

The promotion kicked off on November 23, 2026, which means it’s live right now, and it’ll bag you a free Snom ornament to hang from your Christmas tree - or wherever else you might want to hang it - provided you meet all of the criteria for a qualifying purchase.

The first thing you need to do is make sure you try to get your Snom before it’s too late. The promotion will run until 11:59 pm PST on December 25, 2026, so you have plenty of time. However, that’s only if Pokemon doesn’t run out of Snom ornaments. This is a “while stocks last” situation, and there’s no indication of just how many Snom Pokemon has to go around.

Don't hang around if you missed them the first time. They'll be gone again before you know it.

As long as the deadline hasn’t passed and Pokemon still has them in stock, you will qualify for a free Snom ornament when you spend $50 or more in a single transaction at the Pokemon Center. The only caveat is pre-order and digital products don’t qualify, so no buying stuff that isn’t out yet, and digital versions of games won’t count towards your $50 total.

There is no code to enter at checkout. The Snom ornament should simply be added to your cart when you go to pay and be shipped along with the rest of your order. Just make sure it’s there before you actually check out. The ornaments are limited to one per customer, meaning you won’t get two if you spend over $100, and if you want a refund on anything in your order, the ornament has to be returned along with it.

Pokemon’s holiday collection is now live, so you can shop from that to get your free ornament, and you can also buy all of Pokemon’s Lego sets so far through the Pokemon Center. That includes the Iconic Trainer Moments Poke Ball set which has Red & Blue easter eggs hiding inside. You can get that set for less on Amazon right now, but buying it there means you won’t get your Snom.

Only a week after its best set yet was released, details about three more Pokemon Lego sets have leaked.

#4066. Zenelss Zone Zero Version 2.6 has you playing as an event planner and social media manager for an idol group

Zenelss Zone Zero's Encore for an Old Dream has a good excuse for introducing some new mechanics to the action game.

Zenless Zone Zero’s latest Special Program has delivered a tonne of information about the game’s big upcoming update, Version 2.6. This latest addition kicks off celebrations in New Eridu, and it’s dubbed Encore for an Old Dream.

Version 2.6 is not far off, either, arriving in ZZZ on February 6 - exactly one week from today. Encore for an Old Dream is something of an in-between story that takes place after the end of Season 2.

The narrative of 2.6 sees the Proxies’ return to Sixth Street for New Eridu's annual Gilded Carrot Day. At the centre of the celebrations is the debut of idol group Angels of Delusion at the 404 Error music venue, but not all is as it seems.

The story follows the Proxies getting invited backstage to support the group, which also includes helping them set up practice schedules, organise events and manage social media activities. There’s a rhythm minigame as part of that, along with new maps and mechanics for Marcel Adventure.

Angels of Delusion is also the group that the two new Agents being introduced in this update belong to. Members of the same group are capable of performing coordinated attacks. The new arrivals are Sunna and Aria.

Sunna is a an S-Rank Physical Support Agent who specialises in boosting teammates using Attack and Anomaly. Her Ultimate sees her pull out a giant hammer to land heavy damage, and bring teammates into combat using Quick Assist. Sunna’s companion, Bubblegum, can cast Cat's Gaze on enemies, marking them for detonation. Bubblegum can also buff the squad’s attack.

Aria is the other new arrival, the group’s lead vocalist who can shift between two forms, idol projection and construct. Aria is an Ether Anomaly Agent who also deals high burst damage, specifically against enemies who suffer from any Attribute Anomalies.

Sunna and Aria also benefit from the support of the amusingly named Bangboo Biggest Fan, a fan club president who can heal them over time, and boost the squad’s Attack any time two or more Angels of Delusion members are present.

Version 2.6’s S-Rank re-runs are Yixuan (Auric Ink - Rupture), and Yuzuha (Physical - Support), who you can look forward to as part of the banners.

Version 2.6 will also expand Hollow Zero with a new game mode, Operation Matrix. The mode offers themed stages that rotate weekly, each offering new mechanics. You can now also Sweep in Hollow Zero.

Beyond all the celebrations, this update also brings combat kit overhauls to a couple of older S-Rank characters, Lycaon and Harumasa. You can look forward to multiple limited-time events, too, including one where you can earn a new outfit for Pan Yinhu.

The big event is naturally going to be themed around Gilded Carrot Day, and it actually starts today. There’s the usual run of login rewards (about 3,300 Polychromes), as well as daily activities. Yet another login event - Gilded Surprise, Wonderful Boo-ns - will be available February 14-23, offering daily draws from a pool of 4 billion Polychrome.

As always, there’s no reason not to catch up on the latest set of Zenless Zone Zero codes for some free in-game items.

#4064. Kirby And The World Beyond Details Revealed In Nintendo Catalogue

New details regarding Kirby and the World Beyond have been revealed via Nintendo's winter catalogue in Japan (via Genki_JPN on X). While hardly comprehensive, it provides a little more insight into the game's story along with the abilities and environments available upon its release.

Of course, we know from the debut trailer that this will boast a much broader world than The Forgotten Land, with one detail noting how you can use Kirby's abilities to explore at your own pace. We also get a touch more context behind King Dedede's role, with the article stating that "a mysterious girl" has been kidnapped by the antagonist.

- Use copy abilities to adventure freely in a wide world. - Explore a vast and diverse 3D field with grasslands and waterfalls etc. - Use Kirby’s copy abilities to explore at your own pace. - Kirby’s copy abilities have been powered up! - Ride a Cutter to travel at high speed. - Ride a Bomb and do huge jumps with the blast. - Glide softly through the sky with a Parasol. - A mysterious girl has been captured by King Dedede. - Dedede was sent flying leaving a huge hole in the sky. - “What awaits Kirby beyond other side of the massive wall he destroyed with his newfound powers?”

Kirby and the World Beyond is currently scheduled to launch in Spring 2027. It follows Metroid Ravenous on 28th January 2027, while Xenoblade Genesis and Pokémon Winds & Waves are also expected to launch in the same year.

#4063. Starsand Island is a life and farming sim that isn't gacha, and it's out next week

Starsand Island officially has an Early Access release date, and it sounds like it won't stay there for years.

Though it may seem like we just had a big life sim release in Heartopia, 2026 actually has more than one highly-anticipated release in that particular subgenre of cozy game. The next big one on the horizon is Starsand Island, the life and farming sim from Seed Sparkle Lab.

The game has been gaining momentum since the launch of a demo in October last year, but the developer never quite managed to commit to a date for its debut title. Until now.

Seed Sparkle Lab announced today that Starsand Island will enter Early Access on February 11, which is only a bit over one week from now. This goes for Steam and the Xbox Preview Program version.

The developer said to expect a fairly short Early Access run, as the full launch is expected in the summer of this year. When the full release arrives, the game will also make the jump to PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series, as well as Switch 2.

The full release is also expected to bring Steam Deck support and introduce the multiplayer mode, which will not be available during Early Access

Starsand Island has something of a unique look compared to other games in the subgenre. The storybook, anime-inspired aesthetics are popular in the realm of gacha games, of course. However, seeing as this particular game isn’t gacha, being a premium product means it’s going to offer something free-to-play games aren’t designed to.

Speaking of which, the game will be available in two editions: Standard and Deluxe, with the latter including Romanticism-inspired outfits, furniture, and other customisation items. If you buy either during launch, you’ll also get a Chinese New Year bonus with even more outfits and furniture.

On top of the usual systems of farming, mining, and making friends with adorable characters (and animals), the game also has combat that pits you against ancient guardians. You can, of course, also build a home in it, and decorate it to your heart's content.

Seed Sparkle Lab says you can expect about 100 hours of content in the Early Access launch build, and more features will arrive over the course of the next six or so months, including a crossover event with My Time At Portia.

You can look forward to more Starsand Island coverage from us in the near future. Until then, you can get started by planning who you’re going to date now.

#4062. GTA 6 Smashes Multiple Sales Records And Earns Xbox Series S Praise In First 24 Hours

Update: "Grand Theft Auto VI day one retail sales reached $3.79 billion"

Update [Fri 20th Nov 2026, 10:02pm]: GTA 6 publisher Take-Two is now reporting that day one sales reached $3.79 billion USD, while also selling 32.5 million units pre-release. The $3.79 billion figure is based on "company estimates".

"Rockstar Games, a label of Take-Two Interactive Software, Inc. (NASDAQ: TTWO), is proud to announce that Grand Theft Auto VI day one retail sales reached $3.79 billion, setting a new record for entertainment across any medium, and becoming the biggest entertainment launch in history."

"Achieving a near perfect score of 99 on Metacritic and resounding critical acclaim, Grand Theft Auto VI sold 32.5 million units pre-release, a new record across all platforms."

Original Story: Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 has reportedly smashed all sorts of records within 24 hours of launch, and it's off to a great start on Xbox Series consoles.

As shared by GTA 6 Countdown, GTA 6 has launched to a near-perfect 99 score on Metacritic (151 reviews), apparently sold 24.5m copies in under 24 hours, and seen 2 million Xbox players take a trip to New Zealand to play the game early.

Sensor Tower's sales tracker also estimates $2.36bn (£1.8bn) in revenue from GTA 6 sales, with the console split mostly in favour of PS5, at a 75% to 25% share over Xbox. Still, the data suggests Xbox still took a whopping $588m from 6.15m units sold.

GTA 6 dominated Twitch viewership too, with 50m hours watched and 3.3m viewers during its busiest hour, beating the livestreaming site's previous record (held by Hogwarts Legacy at 1.2m) by more than double.

Beyond all the big numbers we're chucking your way, we've also spotted a lot of praise for the Xbox Series S version of the game. Whilst Digital Foundry was hit-and-miss on the report, the general response online is majorly positive.

It's good news, then, to finally put to bed the lingering question of whether GTA 6 would run well enough on Xbox Series S consoles. Judging by IGN's comparison, it's not all that different of an experience to Sony's flagship PS5 Pro.

Strangely enough, FSR 4.1 still isn't available yet on the Xbox Series X, yet it's already getting very close to PS5 Pro-level performance. Once FSR 4.1 arrives, the Xbox Series X should be able to go toe-to-toe with the PS5 Pro, especially considering that the differences are already quite small today.

The standard PS5, on the other hand, is really starting to show its technical limitations: no VRR below 30 FPS, no Dolby Vision, and a weaker CPU. That makes a noticeable difference in action-heavy scenes and frame rates, since those situations put more strain on the processor.

It also lacks some RDNA 2 features, such as hardware Variable Rate Shading (VRS), relying instead on software-based alternatives.

The Xbox Series X, with its 120Hz VRR support and more powerful CPU, tends to deliver a more stable experience than the original PS5. It just goes to show that Phil Spencer was right: the Xbox Series consoles never needed a mid-gen refresh. They were already ahead of the curve in several key areas, and Rockstar seems to be proving that with GTA 6.

@HonestHick LGs and OLEDs are great, but every TV technology has pros and cons, there isn't a perfect one. E.g. OLED isn't as bright so may not be the best choice in brighter rooms. And for lower frame rates, like 30fps games, it often looks choppier on OLED because the screen is too responsive and you notice it more. OLED amplifies that lower frame rate, whereas LCDs slightly blurring between frames with "sample-and-hold" smooths the transitions. The thing that is bad at high frame rates, becomes a benefit at low frame rates.

Personally I found playing the Switch much less pleasant on my LG OLED, before it broke, and actually ended up playing most Switch games on another TV because of this. (They also looked better on a smaller screen)

But for faster frame rates the motion clarity is much better (on the high end LG models) as are deeper blacks.

@HonestHick As for refunds I probably have a very unpopular take on this. But I don't think we should just be able to get refunds by default if we simply don't like a video game. It's entertainment, and with entertainment you take a risk, sometimes you like it, sometimes you don't. If I go to the theatre, cinema or sporting event and I don't like it, if my team lost, I don't typically get a refund. If I buy a movie and don't like it I don't usually get a refund. Why should we for games?

The one exception for me is performance. If a game doesn't perform well, or makes us motion sick, or similar then yes there should be that option, but I don't think, just because you don't like a game, there should be an expectation of a refund.

Steam is slightly different as every PC runs differently and you may need 2 hours to see if a game works at all on your hardware. Consoles on the other hand everybody gets the same performance. But if a game is broken, or performs poorly on your hardware, e.g. CyberPunk on XBO/PS4, then it should be easier.

#4061. How To Get The Benefactor Schafter S Legendary Car In GTA 6

Here is how to get the Guardia Brothers FRA legendary assault rifle and Benefactor car in GTA 6.

There are a lot of secrets and collectibles hidden throughout Grand Theft Auto 6. These can range from simple easter eggs to comically elaborate puzzles you'll need to solve. However, some just require a bit of criminal activity to earn some great rewards.

Two of these are the Guardia Brothers FRA legendary assault rifle and Benefactor sports car, both of which are obtainable at the same location! If you're looking to snag a few grand, a new car, and a weapon, here is where to find them and how to get these legendary items.

If you want to get this legendary assault rifle and sports car, you will need to first head to Vice City and then go to the Little Cuba district. In the northeast corner of Little Cuba there will be a gated house that a black van will pull into if you get close. This doesn't always happen, and your ability to rob this area isn't determined by the van showing up, so don't fret.

While you can try to just bust through the front gate, you can actually sneak in over the wall. Head to the right of the gate along the spiked wall (shown above) until you reach a section near the back that can be climbed over. I strongly recommend doing this, as you can basically eliminate every gang member without raising an alarm so long as you have a silenced weapon.

Once you reach the backyard, ignore the legendary Benefactor car for now and head up the scaffolding along the side of the building to the roof. Climb through the open hatch and equip your silenced weapon. Below you will be four gang members sitting around a table on the ground floor. Additionally, there is one other criminal rummaging through a safe on the second floor.

Take out your silenced weapon, activate Focus mode, and eliminate all four criminals on the first floor before they can react. If you're fast enough, all of them can be killed without alerting anyone outside or even the guy looking in the safe! With the four gang members dead, use your Focus and look at the floor by the ladder.

This will reveal a secret stash area that has some cash you can loot. There is also a high-end watch on the table to your left along with some Sticky Bombs, which you will need to escape. When you're ready, head down to the second floor and knock out the guy putting money into the safe. Take all the cash and go to the bottom floor.

There you will find a mix of money, marked bills, and jewelry. Stuff your bag full of valuables, loot the bodies, and look for a small armory to the right of the front entrance. In a weapon case, you will find the Guardian Brothers FMA assault rifle. Once you've thoroughly ransacked the place, take everything out the back door to where the Benefactor is.

Store your items in the truck of the car, take out your silenced weapon, and kill the guard who is standing along the driveway near the gate. With him dead, approach the gate at the end of the driveway, attach a sticky bomb to the side when prompted, and shoot the two guards on the other side of the gate. Blow open the gate, then run up to the switch to open the main gate so you can drive out (circled above).

This should allow you to escape without triggering a single gunfight or having the police called on you. Now you can take the Benefactor and get it registered at someone like Moses for a little over $3,800. This ensures you can call the car anytime you need it, making it yours for the rest of the game.

#4060. Nioh 3 launches, immediately becomes the most played Nioh ever on Steam

Just a few hours after launch, Nioh 3 is already the biggest release in series history on Steam.

It sounds like Koei Tecmo’s decision to finally release a Nioh game on PC day-and-date with PlayStation has paid off. The highly-anticipated Nioh 3 has gone live across both platforms, a first for a series that typically spends its initial release months as a console exclusive.

On Steam, and despite having only been available for just a few hours, the game has broken series records, and it continues to climb.

At the time of writing, Nioh 3 has peaked at 42,822 concurrent players on Steam (via SteamDB), and the number keeps going up. Because it’s in the middle of day in Europe and everyone is at work, it’s entirely possible - if not likely - that this figure will get much higher. A weekend bump is also possible, as we’ve seen with several recent releases.

As it stands, the current peak concurrent is enough to get the game in Steam’s top 20 most played games.

This already puts it ahead of all other Nioh games on Steam. The original Nioh peaked at 10,649 when it released in November, 2017. Nioh 2 fared much better, peaking at 41,325 concurrent players in February, 2021.

Of course, you could see that success coming a mile away. The game is currently number one worldwide in Steam’s list of top sellers. This is a jump of 46 positions, for a total of three weeks Nioh 3 has spent in that list.

There are many reasons as to why Nioh 3 has done as well as it has. Word of mouth coming off last year’s PS5-exclusive demo, and the more positive coverage that followed since are just two.

Just last week, Team Ninja released a pretty generous demo across both platforms, which has been well received by players, and likely contributed to sales, in no small part because progress in the demo carries over to the full game.

Critical reviews have been incredibly positive, too. We awarded the game four out of five stars, calling it “Team Ninja’s most accomplished action game, and the series’ most accessible.” It will be interesting to see what number the highest peak concurrent actually settles on over the weekend.

Until then, if you’re jumping in yourself, our Nioh 3 guides are essential reading. Start off with these useful and actually informative gameplay tips, and don’t start playing until you’ve changed these settings. Once you’re ready to get deeper, be sure to read up on how to play co-op with other players, and how to summon AI Acolytes to help you out.

#4059. Exclusive – Behind The Romance: Rockstar Talks GTAVI’s Jason And Lucia

After dozens of hours exploring Leonida, I have a lot of positive things to say about Grand Theft Auto VI, and shared as much in our review of the game. But for my part, the feature that elevated the game most prominently above Rockstar Games’ other (excellent) games wasn’t its graphics, missions, or action – it was the storytelling and interplay between the two lead protagonists. Jason and Lucia bring heart, emotional depth, and a sense of genuine threat to the crime fantasy, as you grow attached to them and start cheering for them against all the odds stacked against them.

We reached out to senior members of the Rockstar Games team to ask about their thoughts on Jason and Lucia, and this is what they had to share.

During my playthrough, the Jason and Lucia dynamic really elevated the experience, adding heart and emotional weight to the expected mix of action, driving, and activities around Leonida. Was a couple or romantic relationship the plan or goal for the game from very early on in development, or did that come later? Do you see the focus on Jason and Lucia’s relationship as one of the features that separates Grand Theft Auto VI from your prior work on storytelling in the game series?

Stephen Donkin, Vice President of Design: “The dual protagonists and the relationship between the two of them was there from very early in development, but exactly how that was expressed in the game did change over time. It was an enormous challenge for us to get them working together in the open world together and finding exactly how that would work. As we started to layer in more mechanics, dialogue, and incremental features across all teams, it just clicked at some point. The ability to be together in the open world also allowed us for new ways to tell the story of the game and to bring some of the exposition and narrative into the open world in a way we hadn’t been able to do before. Hearing these little bits of dialogue as you are just tooling around the world that have specific context to what you as a player have just been doing in the story really knits it all together.”

The player has a choice for how to develop the relationship between the two leads, but I imagine most players are drawn toward helping it thrive. In early playtests, is that what you observed?

Katie Pica, Design Director: Player Systems & Progression:“Overall, we’ve seen that players are invested in supporting Jason and Lucia’s relationship but we don’t favor a specific path through the game, it is completely down to player choice.”

It feels like a lot of the game’s driving narrative beats factor for a close connection between Jason and Lucia. Was it challenging to craft variations that included a more tense or distant connection between the two? Is that even possible?

Luke Howard, Senior Design Director: Missions & Visualization:“One of the core goals of this game was to tell the story of Jason and Lucia with a base line relationship where they are amicable, if just platonic, as they still share the same ultimate goals and need each other to achieve them. So, this gave us a good platform on the main flow to expand particularly intense or emotional moments they experience with variation that can expand on their romantic relationship, while not losing anything if that doesn’t exist. In short, we did develop variation in scenes and interactions that range from subtle to more significant, but done in a way that should feel authentic to the player’s choices, relationship-wise and also criminal profile.

One example is after Lucia helps Kordell’s gang pull off an intense armored truck robbery she shares the information with Raul’s crew. Afterwards Jason pulls Lucia aside to see how she's coping. This moment carries several variations where the performance direction was captured multiple ways to cover a range emotional energy between them. The actors deliveries are brilliant and nuanced – these small tender moments are where we tried to craft pieces that when added up together over the course of the story, author an authentic version of the player’s Jason and Lucia.”

Were there any fictional couples or real-life couples that the team looked at for inspiration in shaping the Jason and Lucia dynamic, whether those couples came from big crime stories or not?

Rupert Humphries, Senior Vice President of Narrative:“We definitely started by looking at all the “couple on the run” movies. There are a lot of them but the ones that we kept coming back to were Warren Beatty and Faye Dunaway in Bonnie and Clyde, McQueen and MacGraw in The Getaway (the Jim Thomson book is also great), True Romance, Thelma and Louise. Clooney and JLo’s dynamic in Out of Sight, as well. And then a lot of buddy movies actually – Riggs and Murtaugh, Butch and Sundance, Mike Lowry and Marcus Burnett, etc. for their back and forth together. In terms of having a game where the characters can change based on how you play and whether you really lean into and enjoy the crime spree we thought about how both Pulp Fiction and Natural Born Killers start with a couple in a diner pulling out guns, but then how different those couples are and how different those scenarios play out. Jason and Lucia are a lot tougher than Tim Roth and Amanda Plummer but we liked the idea of telling a story where Jason and Lucia could end up being closer to either end of that spectrum based on what the player was doing.”

Sex and intimacy are notoriously complicated and challenging to present in games. How did you aim to strike a balance with their private moments together that felt authentic? Any thoughts about how or why it’s so challenging to present adult relationships in video games?

Rupert Humphries, Senior Vice President of Narrative:“This is definitely something we thought a lot about and spent a long time trying to get right. The actors who play Jason and Lucia were so good, and they had a natural chemistry and part of it was just trying to capture some of that.

There’s this trade off in making games between player control and then scripted scenarios. We try and give the player as much control as we can because we are working in an interactive medium and actually doing something rather than watching it is going to feel more powerful. But then you have the ability to really mess around and break the illusion of a tender or romantic moment or whatever it is. So the relationship aspect of this story is there if a player wants to engage in it, but if they don’t the story can play out differently.”

In its best moments of genuine support, regular connection, open communication, and flirty or engagement with one another, Jason and Lucia can come across as a pretty ideal model of good relationships – even while they’re simultaneously committing major crimes together. Was that juxtaposition of a healthy romantic relationship against an external world of illicit activity an explicit goal for how the narrative came together?

Rupert Humphries, Senior Vice President of Narrative:“That was the goal, yes. You are really living with these characters – they’re eating, sleeping, showering, throwing away their trash, or not. The relationship needed to feel real to sit alongside all of that. Then even just as a development team, we live with these characters for years and years. We wanted them to be people we could like, care about, and root for. And they needed to like each other. But then the world itself is so crazy and chaotic and seemingly on the brink of collapse.

When we set out to make this game, and go into that multiyear development marathon, we said we wanted to spend our time working on something with heart, and with some characters you could care about and root for. It’s barely worth even stating, but we are living in a time when people are divided along almost every line, and feelings about the future are pretty bleak. We wanted to create a world that held up a mirror to that, showed that fever pitch of craziness that we are all maybe a couple of bad decisions away from, but we wanted the story we were going to tell to have something positive at its core and the message that human connection is better than division.”

The game automatically moves you to play one character or another at certain points, but for many sequences, you can choose your playable lead. In your experience playing and watching others play, do most players gravitate toward one character or another as “their character?”

Stephen Donkin, Vice President of Design:“It really varied in our playthroughs. They are both such great characters and performances that people seemed to gravitate to both of them in different ways. But overall, we have found the split of time between characters to be relatively even on a per-playthrough and also at a macro level.”

#4058. "Woke Up To A S**t Show" - Binding Of Isaac Dev Shocked To Find GenAI Music In 'Repentance+'

The Binding of Isaac: Repentance+ was one of a handful of games brave enough to launch on 'GTA Day' last week, but while Rockstar has been swimming in positive reception ever since, Isaac's re-release hasn't been so lucky.

Indeed, the game has been subject to a hefty review bombing from players on Steam after it was discovered that AI-generated music was used in the release's new GTA 6-themed online mode (thanks for the heads up, Steam Hype).

A post on the game's Reddit page by user ShweetsStuff alerted players to mentions of the AI music 'tool' Suno in select tracks' metadata, pointing out that no AI disclosure was given on its Steam page (a requirement these days).

As you might expect, players weren't all that happy to learn of the AI usage. At the time of writing, the game's ~1,800 recent reviews lean heavily into the platform's 'Overwhelmingly Negative' camp.

Even the game's original creator, Edmund McMillen, was shocked to learn of the Suno involvement in the game, taking to X to share the following message:

Woke up to a s**t show, obviously I had no idea it featured generated music in the daily run, looking into how that happened and getting it removed, stay tuned.

All fingers point towards publisher Nicalis on this one, then (a company with hardly the best track record when it comes to the treatment of its staff). The studio has since issued a patch on Steam — without any kind of apology, we should add — which removes the GenAI tracks, though it will naturally take longer to make its way to consoles.

What specific skill are we talking about?

Music production has been progressively automating traditional skills for decades through synthesizers/ keyboards, drum machines, MIDI sequencing, virtual instruments, sampling and automated mastering.

Moby took part of a recording from 1960, reversed it and turned it into an internationally successful song. We celebrate that as creative innovation. DJ's have been scratching other people records at the clubs and concerts for decades. People sing and cheer and clap along. AI draws upon existing music to generate something new, we suddenly declare it the death of creativity and its all slop.

Musicians have been drawing inspiration from, adapting and repurposing the work of others for generations. This has literally been happening since music's conception.

Technology changes which skills are necessary. It doesn't eliminate creativity, artistic judgment or the ability to learn. Nor does being a professional musician entitle someone to immunity from technological competition. Did accountants somehow become useless when they stopped counting on their fingers and started using an adding machine? Was there work automatically SLOP, the moment they switched from adding machines to Excel?

Human musicians still have the unique advantage of being able to perform live and connect directly with their audiences. Just like paint to canvas which is something AI wil never do.

Plagiarism is a serious accusation that requires evidence. Simply knowing that something was produced using AI doesn't establish that the resulting work plagiarized another artist.

Similarly, calling something "slop" should be a judgment of its quality, not merely its production method. I havent seen a single person comment about how the song sounded. Just that it was crap because it was AI.

Supporting AI as a creative tool doesn't mean advocating for the elimination of traditional art. Both can coexist.

And while you're expanding your ignore list, make sure you're applying your principles consistently. You might want to stop listening to every musician who has ever "borrowed" a melody, sampled another artist's recording or repurposed someone else's work.

If drawing from existing art is inherently wrong, that standard should apply to everyone, not just those using AI. Otherwise, you're being rather selective about what you consider acceptable creative expression.

#4057. Why Do I Want To Paint The Walls In Grand Theft Auto VI?

I admire the cozy sim genre. Stardew Valley and Animal Crossing are on regular rotation in my home on my family’s screens, but not my own. In an odd way, I find the genre stressful, arguably the opposite of its intended purpose. I will happily and cathartically guide Grace Ashcroft through the tense hallways of Rhodes Hill in Resident Evil Requiem, but Pokémon Pokopia’s seemingly endless list of to-dos makes me sweat. It’s just not my genre, and I have come to terms with that.

Grand Theft Auto VI is not a cozy game, but it has a substantial amount of cozy elements and mechanics. Bird (and animal) watching, for example, is apparent and encouraged early in the experience. You can also fix up your somewhat dilapidated home from almost the moment you are let loose outside of the opening tutorial missions.

And for some reason, I couldn’t start that process fast enough.

I climbed to the roof to fix the leak and replaced all the stairs leading up to the home before I ever participated in the game’s namesake and stole a car. Normally, it’s the kind of interaction I skip or choose not to engage with, given the option. Or, I do the bare minimum to progress. Sure, I have all the options in the world to build and decorate a house and make it my own, but… that feels like a lot of work. And I am not an artist.

The “cozy” elements of Grand Theft Auto VI are admittedly different from those in a game like Pokopia or Animal Crossing. You’re not designing your home (though you can pick a paint color), but it feels similar, and I am trying to figure out why I enjoy it here as opposed to other games. Is it because Jason and Lucia are so instantly believable as human beings that I want their home to be nicer?

After some thought, I think it might just come down to Grand Theft Auto VI’s consistently impressive visual fidelity. Replacing the shingles on the roof, for example, offers a close-up look at Jason’s character model, and you can practically feel the texture of the asphalt while the heat of the sun beats down.

I don’t have confirmation, but it also just feels like someone at Rockstar did exhaustive research on what the process of replacing a roof shingle should look like, even if, I’m sure, it probably doesn’t quite work that way in the real world. Jason makes it look incredibly easy, to the point that it had me questioning if I should be climbing up to my own roof and taking care of some loose shingles myself. And you know what is a lot of fun? Watching someone who is good at something do the thing they’re good at.

I’m now into the driving and shooting part of the game (and enjoying that, too!), but I am shocked at how grateful I was to have the option to stay home and put up drywall.

#4056. Honkai: Star Rail Version 4.0 brings a new world, and a Fortnite collaboration

Honkai: Star Rail's next major update introduces a whole new planet to the RPG, and way more besides.

HoYoverse just wrapped up a big Honkai: Star Rail Special Program. We’ve been waiting for this one for a couple of weeks now thanks to a delay, but the developer has finally delivered all the news on Version 4.0, which will arrive February 13.

The upcoming major release is dubbed No Aha at Full Moon for a very good reason. Aha's Planarcadia is the big new world headlining Version 4.0.

Planarcadia is a place whose description sounds a bit like a Warhammer 40,000 Eldar homeworld, and is quite open about its cyberpunk inspirations. In-universe, however, it was born out of the pages of an art canvas, and it’s a world where pleasure is king.

The squad’s host in this chapter is Madam Pearl, who will oversee the the Astral Express’ return to the place where they first began their journey. Duomension City is where you’re going to land, and meet the creatures that dwell in this world.

The imagenae of Planarcadia require attention to survive, and they feed off people’s Wishpower. If they don’t get any attention, they perish, which does tie into the general themes of the place. Duomension City has other interesting locations that you’re going to visit, such as the Graphia Academy art school, the commercial district of Dovebrook, and a few other places hidden behind mysterious entrances.

The Phantasmoon Games is another highlight of Planarcadia, a competitive spectacle where you’ll have a chance to compete to become Aeon for a Minute. If you make it to the final stages, you may earn an audience with The Laughter.

Much like the world where the games take place, the whole point of the competition is to attract the most attention, so rules are a bit loose as to how you manage to do that. The event will bring together several of the game’s factions, though not everyone is there for the competition.

As you explore Planarcadia, if you have characters on your team who are on the newly-playable Path of Elation, you’ll earn Punchlines. The more you accumulate, the closer you get to catching Aha’s attention, which triggers Aha Instant.

Version 4.0 introduces two new 5-Star characters to Honkai: Star Rail. General Yao Guang (Madam Yao) is one, a Seer Strategist from the Xianzhou Alliance's Yuque. If you’ve been playing the game, you may already be familiar with her voice, as she's previously been in touch with our heroes via radio link. But V4.0 marks her first on-screen appearance, as well as her playable debut.

General Yao Guang is a Physical character on the Path of Elation whose specialty is using Weal and Woe Lots in battle, which she uses to increase Elation for allies, and grant everyone Punchline any time she uses a Skill. If an Aha Instant is triggered, she casts Woe Lots, which debuff enemies, causing them to take increased damage, all while regenerating Skill Points for the rest of the team.

Her aptly named Certified Banger buff adds one extra instance of Elation to teammates’ attacks. And her Ultimate grants the team Punchline, and triggers an extra Aha Instant.

The other new arrival is likewise a Path of Elation devotee. Sparxie is a suspiciously familiar streamer who uses her influencer skills in combat. When she fights, she turns the fight into a battle for attention, as she forces enemies to engage in a race for upvotes.

When you consume Skill Points, Sparxie will get gifts, which in turn cause her to regenerate Skill Points and Punchlines for the team. You can continue doing this to increase your damage. When Aha Instant is triggered, Sparxie unleashes a lucky draw that deals damage to enemies with each bounce.

She also benefits from the Certified Banger state, which causes the gifs she receives to deal more Elation damage to a random enemy target. Her Ultimate also deals more Elation damage.

Version 4.0 will see a few re-runs, too. Black Swan, Evernight, and Hysilens will be part of the first half's Warp events. The second half will see the return of Sparkle, Cerydra, and Rappa — that's right, HoYoverse have finally remembered Rappa exists, after one of the longest rerun waits in the game's history! Both Black Swan and Sparkle are getting a few tweaks to their kit with this version, too, so the timing works.

If you log in after launch, you’ll get 20 free pulls and a new free outfit for Ruan Mei. If you play while the Yao Guang fortune event is active, you could earn 1,600 Stellar Jades. You can also expect a free 5-Star character selector to arrive at some point after launch, giving you a free choice between popular (but admittedly a bit old for the meta these days) limited-banner characters Jing Yuan, Kafka, Dan Heng • Imbibitor Lunae, Jingliu, Sparkle, Acheron, and Aventurine.

Finally, the other major news is a Fortnite collaboration. Starting February 26, Kafka and Blade will join Epic’s battle royale shooter. On that day, you’ll find skins of the two Stellaron Hunters in the Fortnite Item Shop, and the new outfits are even compatible with Fortnite's LEGO styles. You can also expect other customisation bits like Back Bling, Pickaxe, and more to be part of the package.

If you download the game on the Epic Games Store, and take part in Honkai: Star Rail-themed activities, you’ll also get the Blade character outfit in Fortnite for free. Event schedule and timing will be announced at a later date.

#4055. Where To Find GTA 6's The Last Of Us Easter Egg

There are more secrets, references, and easter eggs in GTA 6 than we can possibly know. We will almost certainly be stumbling on them for years to come. A lot have been discovered during these first few days, though, including what is almost certainly a friendly jab at Naughty Dog for its many remasters and remakes of The Last of Us games.

There are electronics stores dotted all over Leonida, but on the shelves of one called Game Horde that can be found in the Port Gellhorn region of the map, there are video games. Not video games that exist in our world, or would even be compatible with our consoles, but all are references to real games and compatible with the JoySystem, the in-universe console you can play back at your house after Cal sets it up in the early stages of the game.

There are a few games on the shelf, most of which appear to be GTA 6 versions of real-life titles, although the most obvious is the We Came Together collection. Not only do the name and the font confirm that it's the Vice City version of The Last of Us, but Rockstar has had a little fun at Naughty Dog’s expense with the easter egg.

Under the game name along the case’s spine, it reads “I, II, & III Remasters of the Remakes”. Clearly a little dig at Naughty Dog for repeatedly re-releasing the first two Last of Us games rather than making a new one. The Last of Us has a rematser and a remake, The Last of Us Part 2 has already been remastered, and both Part 1’s remake and Part 2’s remaster were re-released as a double-pack.

You might argue that it’s pretty rich of Rockstar to make that joke when it released GTA 5 across three different consoles, it just never gave its GTA 6 predecessor the remaster label. Even when taking that into account, though, Naughty Dog has given its games more remasters and remakes, even though the original The Last of Us was released only three months before GTA 5.

The GTA 6 equivalent of The Last of Us Part 3 is also already available in Leonida. We’ll be waiting another decade for the real thing, at least.

The other JoySystem games on the shelf are Desolate Rim, which is Death Stranding based on the font, Righteous Slaughter is GTA’s Call of Duty, and Glory Souls 2. Clearly a FromSoftware game, but it’s unclear which one. The name suggests Demon’s Souls, but the font screams Elden Ring.

GTA 6 players have spent almost 80,000 years collectively in-game already, so it’s no wonder these tiny details are already being discovered. What’s even more remarkable, considering that timeframe, is how much more we still haven’t seen.

We know it's been a long wait for GTA 6, but when you think about it, we've all lived so many lives since GTA 5.

#4054. Talking Point: What Are You Playing This Weekend? (November 21-22)

Welcome back, PX'ers! You know the drill by now: it's time to talk with us about what you're playing this weekend.

I'm fully expecting the comments section to be flooded with GTA 6 this and GTA 6 that. Totally understandable behaviour. So, I'll keep this WAYP brief. Be sure to check out our Black Friday sales roundup later today and let us know what you pick up!

Alrighty then, let's get into it. Here's what we're playing on Xbox this weekend:

GTA 6, right? No surprise that's what I'm going to be playing. Fraser had a monumental blast with the game, and talking with him about it has given me the biggest case of FOMO going. Woof.

Other than the obvious, I've been playing a lot of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Well, I say playing, more like learning songs on the in-game ocarina. I learned how to play Orbiter by Noah Kahan because I went to see the lad play the London O2 this week. I made a silly Instagram Reel of what it was like to learn the song, if you're interested. It was really fun.

I've also been thoroughly enjoying co-oping It Takes Two and SONIC PICO PARK with my beloved. So, we'll probably play some more of those.

#4053. Grand Theft Auto VI's Auto Drive Is A Beautiful And Free Version Of Hands-Free Travel

Grand Theft Auto VI is a game where you spend a lot of time behind the wheel. Always has been. But sometimes, you just won't feel like actively driving, but you also don't to waste money on a cab.

This is where Auto Drive comes in. It lets the game take over and drive you where you need to go in real time and all with a cinematic camera that shifts and moves, letting you take in the environment without all that pesky "having to pay attention to the road." Red Dead Redemption 2 had the same feature, and I have fond memories of taking advantage of it to watch Arthur ride his horse through that game's incredible environment. It's a great option in GTAVI, but how to use it and turn it on isn't immediately apparent.

First, you must select a destination. Get the GPS set up to direct you to where you want to go.

Next, start driving. The Auto Drive is smart, but doesn't seem to be smart enough to make three-point turns or back out of parking lots. You need to be on your way before you can turn it on.

Once you're on the path, hold down in the d-pad and press start to activate Cinematic.

Once you've done this you should be able to hold down the Circle button on PlayStation or the B button on Xbox to activate Auto Drive and... voilà! You can sit back and let Jason or Lucia take the wheel. They will drive legally, even stopping at lights, but you can speed them up if they're taking too long.

I've always enjoyed driving in Grand Theft Auto, but I was grateful to find this almost-hidden option early in the game.

#4052. Heartopia shows off My Little Pony collaboration, and there's a pre-launch event to hold you over

Heartopia’s My Little Pony collaboration is close, and the pre-launch event has already kicked off.

Heartopia has officially shared initial details about its first-ever collaboration event. The game, which launched a month ago to great success on mobile, as well as Steam on PC, has already been a staple among fans of Animal Crossing and The Sims.

Things are kicking into gear, it seems, because the game is already about to host its first collaboration event, and it is with My Little Pony.

The Heartopia X My Little Pony event officially begins on February 14, but a pre-launch login event is now live through the actual collaboration’s start. The limited-time event offers players sign-in puzzles every day that will unlock time-limited Exhibition Passes.

The first actual piece of My Little Pony-themed content can be yours if you complete all puzzles, as that gets you a limited edition costume for your pet, based on the show’s Spike. The event itself, which will be available until March 15, brings My Little Pony’s Tree of Harmony into the world of Heartopia.

The ponies need your help to Wield Elements of Harmony so they can reawaken the tree, and bring it back to Equestria. In gameplay terms, you’re going to want to perform daily sensing at the tree in order to earn three of the six Elements of Harmony: Honesty, Generosity, Loyalty, Kindness, Laughter, and Magic.

The more you do this, the more the tree’s Energy goes up, and the more rewards and resources you stand to earn. Even more time-limited Exhibition Passes, and Moonlight Crystals can be earned as you water the tree.

Badge Pull Tokens are your big reward, which is what you’re actually going to use to get the special Pony Series badges. You’ll earn ten time-limited Exhibition Passes each time you complete one of the three sets of Pony Series badges. Collect all three and you’ll earn Town Collaboration Series badges.

Heartopia is a free-to-play game, so you know there is a Gacha component to this event. Expect six non-replacement Gacha Pools that each map to one member of My Little Pony’s Mane Six. Within each pool, you’ll be able to earn five outfit pieces, and one vehicle.

If any of that sounds interesting, definitely log in now to play the pre-launch event, which should hold you over until the proper show kicks off Saturday. If you’re already enjoying Heartopia, you likely want to learn about Onsen Egg Promise locations, Fish locations, and Bug locations - all of which can be found at those links.

We also recently updated our guides on how to catch Frostspore fish - and if you’re into cooking, how to obtain every recipe and variant. If you haven’t already, definitely see if you missed any of these Heartopia codes, too.
